title: Common prayer
hookLine: the same prayers said together across the world

cards: Why does the Lord's Prayer start with "our"? "Our Father which art in heaven." Jesus could have taught "my Father."

Even when someone prays it alone, on the edge of a bed at midnight, the first word is plural. The prayer assumes company. The Church of England put the idea on its prayer book's cover: the Book of Common Prayer.
Common, as in shared. The same words, on the same day, in one parish and the next and the next. Today: common prayer.

teach.h: KOINONIA: A LIFE HELD IN COMMON.
teach.b: In Acts, just after Pentecost, the first believers are described like this: "they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." Prayers they kept together.
The Greek word behind fellowship there is koinonia: sharing, a life held in common. Common prayer reaches for the same thing.

In the prayer book, each Sunday and holy day has its own short prayer called a collect, set out through the whole church year. So on a given Sunday, a village church and a city church miles away pray the same collect.
A collect speaks to God, remembers something God has done, asks for one thing, and closes through Christ.

Here's the one for the second Sunday in Advent: "Blessed Lord, who hast caused all holy Scriptures to be written for our learning; Grant that we may in such wise hear them, read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest them."
Inwardly digest: a whole way of reading in one breath.
Some who pray this way describe a quiet gift: on a day with no words of one's own, or no strength to mean them, other voices hold the prayer up, and another day the favor is returned.

teach.h: WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED.
teach.b: Jesus makes a promise sized for a small room as much as a cathedral: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Christians pray in more than one way.
Some prefer their own words in the moment; churches with a prayer book or set liturgy lean on shared texts. Either way, the first word is still our.

how: In Anglican churches each Sunday and holy day has an appointed collect, prayed near the start of the service, and the prayer book directs the Sunday collect to be used again through the week that follows at Morning and Evening Prayer.

games.q: it's a hard morning. you're too tired to find words of your own, and you want to pray. what does common prayer offer you?
o: wait until the feeling comes back.
lean on the day's collect, the words others are saying with you.
games.why: the prayer book gives a collect for each Sunday and holy day, so on a tired morning you can lean on shared words. other voices hold the prayer up for a while.

practice: Take this week's collect, or the old one from the communion service: Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid.

If you pray, say it slowly, aloud or inside, holding in mind the others saying words like these today, in a cathedral, a hospital chapel, a kitchen; if you don't, simply listen to the words and keep the others in mind.

wordCard.voice: Common prayer. The same prayers, said together by people who may never meet, from one shared book and one shared year.

orig.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing, having in common — the word behind "fellowship" in Acts 2:42.

carryVoice: Your line: prayer in common. Words shared across many rooms. Go gently.
